items.question: How do you think about the trade-offs involved in choosing model sizes for Llama?

There's so many parameters to take into account: the scaling laws, the training time to get the best performance, the GPU constraint, and on what different hardware. We think about Meta, but also the community, and people are not just using H100, but A100, different sizes of GPUs and memory. So which size will fit in what, and what is the most useful also at inference time, not just at fine-tuning time? Then you can maybe do some tricks at inference time to quantize it a bit, or FP16 or FP8 now. All those constraints make it very, very challenging. At inference time you have a lot of costs. So how to trade off between inference cost and training cost? It's a very challenging problem. Llama 2, maybe I would say it's like Llama 1. We had a flagship model which was 70B. What would be the right balance to still fit in a different size? So, we try to have some trade-off like that.

items.question: How do you think about Chinchilla’s scaling laws when choosing the size and training budget of a model people will use at inference time?
items.object: Chinchilla scaling laws and the trade-off between training efficiency and inference efficiency
items.answer: There was the Kaplan paper with scaling laws, but they figured out—basically, they tried two dimensions: the model weights and the number of training time, like number of steps, training tokens, epochs. And for that they figured out that model size is what matters. So, GPT-3 was way too big compared to the actual number of train tokens because they made a mistake not adapting the scheduler. That's what Chinchilla emphasized and discovered. To be fair, I think OpenAI knew that at the time of the Chinchilla paper, but, yeah, basically Chinchilla said we have to revisit the scaling laws that were originally published by Kaplan and emphasize much more the importance of training tokens. And they did some really good scaling laws showing that there's an optimal ratio: basically, you need to double the number of train tokens every time you double the training weights to get an optimal ratio, so that for a finite number of compute you will end with the best results in your paper. And what I call the Chinchilla trap is that that's good if you want the best flagship model that obtains the highest performance on your paper. But if you want to use your model at inference time, inference has two dimensions: one remains, the model weights, but one drops, the number of tokens you train it, number of steps. And so, to be compute-efficient at inference time, it's much better to train it much longer, even if it's an additional effort, than to have a bigger model. That's what I call the Chinchilla trap. Not that Chinchilla was wrong, but if you consider inference time, you need to go beyond Chinchilla. And in fact, that's what Llama 1 folks did by overtraining, in the sense they could have gotten a better performance in the paper, but they preferred to create the best artifact that will be used by the community. So, that's the scaling thinking.

items.question: Why are you excited about using tool-augmented language models to generate synthetic data for post-training?
items.object: Synthetic data from tool-augmented language models for post-training
items.answer: I think it's very different from pre-training, and it's the future direction on synthetic data that I'm personally excited about. For instance, we had this survey on augmented LLMs a year ago. And all the idea is, if you augment your LLM with something else, it can be a retriever, search, a tool, a calculator, code execution. Then you are not just distilling, doing some data augmentation with your model, but you're actually adding some expert skills that possibly go beyond the model weights. For instance, if your model can calculate something—it was wrong before, and now it has access to a calculator and you can retrain your model on that. Then you're learning something new. If your model didn't know something about Llama 2, it probably doesn't know a lot about Llama 3. But now if it can search online about it and then you train the model on that, then you have a positive feedback loop, what we call expert direction, targeting directly the weakness of the model. It's continual augmentation of the language model much beyond just that augmentation.

items.question: Why do you see tool-assisted self-correction as a promising direction for language models to keep learning?
items.object: Tool-assisted self-correction as a direction for continued language-model learning
items.answer: What I said is more like in terms of directions, not for Llama 3, but when it knows how to use a tool and correct itself, this is a very promising direction that goes much beyond augmentation for the future, to keep collecting new data and new tokens. People are saying we're lacking tokens. But if you think about those kinds of tokens where the model always goes to correct its own weakness, it can say, 'Okay, that's 10 + 10.' That's an easy example, probably the model knows, but imagine something more complex. '10 + 10, I expect this to be 20. items.question: How did your experience training Llama 2 change your understanding of why reinforcement learning with human feedback works?

items.answer: When we started Llama 2, I had this budget of annotations in millions of dollars and, okay, what do you do? I'm responsible for that. I'm accountable for a model at the end that can follow instructions and compete with GPT-3.5 at the time. You can annotate supervised fine-tuning data, which refers to a human creating a prompt and also writing the answer expected by the model. So then you train on that in a supervised manner. The other thing is reinforcement learning with human feedback, where the annotators type a prompt, but this time you sample two different answers from your model and ask the annotator which one they prefer. And then you train on the preference, basically, to simplify. That seems very weird and not really robust, training on synthetic output generated by the model. So I was like, let's annotate 100,000 more supervised fine-tuning data and let's annotate a bit of preference to do a little check because everyone is doing it. And we had this human evaluation after a few weeks in the Llama 2 project where our model was already better than the annotation from the humans. So you'd get a prompt, you'd check what the human would have annotated as an answer. You check what the model generates and most of the time the model was better. I was like, oh, maybe the annotators are pretty bad. Let's look at that. And no, the model was pretty good. And so I understood the intuition behind RLHF. Those models are already super good at some tasks. Imagine a distribution, a Gaussian distribution. You have on the left bad outputs and on the right good outputs. And the same way, like medical diagnostics from a doctor: you have good outputs on the right and bad diagnostics on the left. When you collect all the diagnostics from doctors, hopefully it's mostly on the right, but humans make mistakes, right? On the left, you still have a bit of examples. And the same way for humans, they make mistakes when they annotate, and so training on behavioral cloning to reflect humans, the model will learn to make some mistakes, just like humans. And you cannot go beyond that if you train on human outputs. But now, if I ask a doctor to check two diagnostic answers, one is better than the other. It's easy for a doctor to say which one is better. The same way, if I sample from my model that learns the human distribution of answers, there's one bad time to time like humans, but most of the time good answers, and I ask a human to choose which one they prefer. Personally, I'm really bad at creating poems. The example I give a lot of the time: try to write a haiku in three lines about language models. Take like 5 seconds to think what could come. I'm terrible. But yet, if I check two poems generated by a model or human, I can tell which one I prefer. I'm good at discriminating. And because of that, you can have a model that flattens the bad outputs and learns to only shift towards the best and better and better outputs. And you can even end up with superhuman abilities, since I'm bad at writing a poem, but I'm good at judging which one is better. So, I can actually annotate data beyond my own skills at creating them. That's the magic of RLHF.

items.question: How do you think about choosing between RLHF and supervised fine-tuning for training models to write code?
items.object: RLHF versus supervised fine-tuning for code
items.answer: That's an open research question. The intuition in general is that, for instance, for code, because this is factual, you can check if the code is correct or not, RLHF is not the way to go. You prefer to do supervised fine-tuning, as a human writing the code. But in fact, because humans make mistakes, because even in code there are some preferences that emerge like that, and maybe for some other reasons that we don't know, RLHF is so much more scalable, it costs less, it's easier, and then it leads in general to just better performance. And maybe we can come up with a compromise. We actually suggested a new method in Llama 3, teacher critic, where it reconciles and unifies supervised fine-tuning and RLHF such that when you do human preference and you have two outputs, but both are very bad in the code, for instance, you will ask the human to edit the best answer to make it correct now. So now you're doing SFT when all the answer was really bad such that you can get out from the local minimum of your model.

items.question: How do you approach evaluating language models during post-training as their capabilities improve?
items.object: Evaluation of language models during post-training
items.answer: There's no good answer. Evals are an open research problem, in particular when you're trying to tackle so many capabilities. As soon as you're trying to push numbers on a benchmark, it stops being a good benchmark because then you don't know if you're overfitting it and it will transfer to similar capabilities. So, evaluation for language models, in particular on post-training, is a very hard problem. We tackle that by playing with different methods like reward model evaluation, model as a judge, having a diversity of prompts, diversity of benchmarks as well for a lot of different capabilities. That limits the possibility of hacking them, of course. We also do a lot of human evaluation. I do a lot of model test quality analysis, testing myself some prompts. I feel it was much easier during Llama 2 when the model was worse than today. Now the models are getting so good that it's hard to get prompts to break them and compare models and see their edge cases. So, it's getting harder. And a great way also to compare models is through the different rounds we have done for RLHF. We upload a new model. For all the annotation we are doing, we have the win rate between the previous model and the new model by just sampling for every prompt we annotate. Prefer sample A with the old model, sample B with the new model. And so, we can calculate a win rate automatically.

items.question: How would you like language-model evaluations to account for a model's ability to say it doesn't know?

items.question: How do you think about the tradeoffs involved in increasing Llama 3's tokenizer vocabulary?
items.object: Llama 3's larger tokenizer vocabulary
items.answer: There's a lot of dimensions to take into account here, I think. The first obvious thing to say is Llama 3 compared to Llama 2 is multilingual, has multilingual capabilities. We worked on that. And so, because you have languages that are not just Latin languages like English, there's a lot of different characters. You want to include them to represent special words there. And so, you need to have a bigger vocabulary size. That's the obvious thing, which is also probably why GPT-4o has a much bigger vocabulary, as it's naturally multilingual, multimodal, and speech. So, that's why we went from 32 to 128 vocabulary size. The interesting thing to discuss about the tokenizer is scaling laws related to that. If you increase your vocab size, you have a bigger matrix, which takes longer to compute. It depends on the model size, but for a small model, it has a much bigger impact than for a bigger model. As a relative percentage of the total number of weights for the 7B, it's much more than the 405B. So, that has more impact in terms of training speed there. But what is interesting is with a bigger vocabulary, for the same text, you have fewer tokens, right? And so, you can train your model on the same amount of knowledge with fewer steps. For the same compute, you can see more knowledge if you don't keep up. That's one cool thing. The second thing is at inference time, the context length is not in number of text or the size of the text, but number of tokens. And so, you can compress more such that with a bigger tokenizer, 128 more vocabulary, you can get to longer text for the same number of tokens.

items.question: How do you judge whether an AI startup’s business will remain valuable as models improve?
items.object: AI startup strategy as deep learning models improve
items.answer: That's a tough question. One thing I say quite often is deep learning has these very specificities that make it challenging to predict. It's self-descriptor, self-destructive technology. Something like Grammarly, this technology where the startup—you plug and play and it corrects your grammatical errors. Everyone told them, 'Guys, deep learning creates a barrier to entry: annotate data, create data.' And they had a lot of data for that. And the next day, with the same exact technology, deep learning, someone comes with ChatGPT in Poland and can do the same better and so many other things. Zero barrier to entry from yesterday to today. And what is crazy here is that it's based on the same technology. And so, there's a lot of people working nowadays to try to mitigate issues with current-generation models. And I'm telling them, assume always the next generation will get better. So, if your business will benefit from a new generation with better abilities, that's a good business. If your business may be replaceable, and all the work you have done may vanish and be wasted because there are better models, then maybe change.
